set.body:
RAISED AS A QUESTION, NOT AN ASSERTION. Two independent analyses of the same quantity have recorded different constants, and one of them is about to be documented.

THE DISAGREEMENT. The evidence-sampling-v1 contract note on bd-01KZY9FGVJ0JXCB1Q1KN88AE6D records, verbatim:

  "records sqrt(M+1) for the actual sample-SD-across-edges recipe"

The independent analysis that produced the original finding derived sqrt(M-1) as the asymptotic ratio of the true sampling SD to the naive across-pairs SE in the signal-dominated limit, from Diedrichsen Eq. 35: the signal term decays as 1/M and the noise term as 1/(M(M-1)), while a naive across-pairs SE scales as 1/(M(M-1)) throughout.

THE EMPIRICAL DATA, from 4000 Monte Carlo replicates per cell at the largest effect size tested:

  M (partitions)        3      4      6      8      12
  observed ratio      1.92   2.05   2.41   2.73   3.25
  sqrt(M-1)           1.41   1.73   2.24   2.65   3.32
  sqrt(M+1)           2.00   2.24   2.65   3.00   3.61

  residual vs sqrt(M-1)   +0.51  +0.32  +0.17  +0.08  -0.07     converging
  residual vs sqrt(M+1)   -0.08  -0.19  -0.24  -0.27  -0.36     diverging

The observed ratio CONVERGES on sqrt(M-1) as M grows and diverges from sqrt(M+1). sqrt(M+1) fits better only at M=3, where the asymptotic regime has not been reached.

THREE POSSIBILITIES, and I cannot distinguish them from outside:

  1. The two constants describe DIFFERENT QUANTITIES. sqrt(M+1) may be the exact finite-sample
     factor for a specific sample-SD recipe - for instance one using an N rather than N-1
     denominator over the C(M,2) edges, or one that includes the edge count differently -
     while sqrt(M-1) is the asymptotic ratio of true SD to naive SE. Both could be correct
     statements about different things.
  2. sqrt(M-1) is the asymptote and sqrt(M+1) is an exact finite-M expression that happens to
     approach a different limit, in which case one of the two derivations has an error.
  3. One is simply wrong.

Note also that the original characterisation of the empirical curve as approaching sqrt(M-1)
"from below" is incorrect in direction - the observed values approach it from ABOVE, crossing
near M=12. That looseness is mine to own and is a reason to treat the whole comparison with care
rather than a reason to prefer either constant.

WHY THIS IS WORTH RAISING BEFORE THE DOCS SHIP. The closure note says docs now state that pair
rows are dependent estimator contributions and that full covariance replaces the spread-across-
edges SE. If a numerical constant accompanies that guidance, it will be read as authoritative and
copied. A user computing sqrt(M+1) where sqrt(M-1) is correct at M=12 would be off by 11 percent
in the SE - not catastrophic, but wrong, and wrong in a package whose entire argument is that its
quantities are better defined than the alternatives.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT. Evaluate both expressions against the exact Eq. 13 diagonal at several M
with a fixed metric, symbolically or numerically, rather than against simulation. The Eq. 13
diagonal is 4*d*Xi/(M*P) + 2*Xi^2/(M*(M-1)*P); the naive across-pairs SE has a closed form; the
ratio of the two is exact and needs no Monte Carlo. Whoever owns evidence-sampling-v1 is better
placed to do that than I am, since they have already implemented the oracle.

I am not proposing a change to the implementation. The exported covariance was verified
independently and its coverage is nominal - this concerns only the documented recipe constant for
users who compute a spread across edges anyway.
set.title: Two independent derivations disagree on the across-edges SE constant: sqrt(M-1) vs sqrt(M+1)
